title: Set Notation and Conditional Probability

findings.finding: Extend part a to examine how shared elements affect the number of distinct elements in a union.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects counting distinct elements with the effect of adding an element already in the union.
findings.checked: For A={1,3,5} and B={3,5,7}, n(A)+n(B)=6 and n(A∪B)=4. Adding 1 to B leaves the union unchanged. All required set notation and methods are taught before this question.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up for students who finish early.

repair.proposal: After p12-q22-a add: (i) Find n(A)+n(B). Answer: 6. (ii) How much greater is this than n(A∪B)? Answer: 2. (iii) If 1 is added to B, find the new n(A∪B). Answer: 4. (iv) Explain why adding 1 to B leaves the union unchanged. Answer: 1 was already in A and therefore already in the union.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts use the original sets and include the expected answers.

findings.finding: The identification task introduces set subtraction without defining it.
findings.breakdown: Students must interpret subtraction between sets rather than between their cardinalities. Earlier teaching defines union, intersection and complement, but does not explain this additional operation.
findings.checked: The complete preceding teaching, including p7-demonstrations-o-r, contains no definition or demonstration of set subtraction. The region labels in p13-regions-definition do not explain the minus sign.
findings.assumptions: The supplied booklet teaching is the written preparation; teacher-led delivery does not supply the missing definition automatically.

repair.proposal: Before p13-l add: “For sets, X−Y contains the elements in X that are not in Y. Here, start with A∪B and remove the region A∩B.”

findings.doneWhen: Set subtraction is explained before students interpret p13-l.

findings.finding: The worked example substitutes the counts 50, 19 and 9 without showing how they arise from the event descriptions.
findings.breakdown: The example leaves the selection of the intersection unwritten, including the decision to exclude 20. Students see the addition formula applied without a model of how its numerical inputs were obtained.
findings.checked: The counts are mathematically correct. Earlier numerical-set tasks supply relevant experience, but neither they nor this example explicitly connect these three substituted values to their event selections. Under the worked-example standard, their origins must be stated.
findings.assumptions: Calculator access does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Before the substitution add: “A contains the 50 even numbers 2, 4, …, 100. B contains the 19 numbers 1, 2, …, 19. A∩B contains the 9 even numbers 2, 4, …, 18.”

findings.doneWhen: Each substituted numerator has an explicit origin, including why the intersection ends at 18.

findings.finding: Extend question 6 with a controlled comparison that holds the marginal probabilities fixed while varying the overlap.
findings.breakdown: Increasing the overlap decreases the union and increases neither. The existing parts compare different set relationships but do not provide a consecutive three-case run with fixed marginal probabilities.
findings.checked: The proposed intersection probabilities 0, 1/6 and 1/3 are all feasible with marginals 1/2 and 1/3. The resulting union and complement probabilities are correct. Addition and complement methods are taught on p21.
findings.assumptions: The new cases are separate parts of question 6, each with its own givens; the diagram and fixed intersection in part c do not apply to them.

repair.proposal: After q6(c), add further parts under the existing “Find” instruction, requesting P(A∪B) and P(overline{A∪B}) in each case. Add only this instructional line: “Predict how each answer will change before calculating.” (d) P(A)=1/2, P(B)=1/3, P(A∩B)=0. Answers: 5/6, 1/6. (e) P(A)=1/2, P(B)=1/3, P(A∩B)=1/6. Answers: 2/3, 1/3. (f) P(A)=1/2, P(B)=1/3, P(A∩B)=1/3. Answers: 1/2, 1/2. Follow with (g) P(A)=3/5, P(B)=1/4, P(A∩B)=1/10. Answers: 3/4, 1/4. In d–f only the intersection varies.

findings.doneWhen: The three comparison cases and unpatterned follow-up appear as independent parts without altering the existing diagrams or givens.

findings.finding: Part e supplies impossible probability data, but the shared instruction permits only dependent or independent classifications.
findings.breakdown: An intersection probability of 0.8 cannot occur with marginal probabilities 0.2 and 0.4. Applying the preceding product comparison mechanically would label nonexistent events dependent.
findings.checked: Since A∩B is contained in each event, its probability cannot exceed either marginal. The preceding independence examples use valid data and do not introduce an impossible-data response. The supplied answer recognises impossibility, but students cannot see that answer as instruction.
findings.assumptions: The impossible case is retained as a validity check within the classification task.

repair.proposal: Append to the shared instruction: “If the probabilities cannot describe events, state this instead. An intersection probability cannot exceed either individual event probability.”

findings.doneWhen: The instruction allows students to identify part e as impossible and supplies the needed validity check.

findings.finding: Hold the intersection probability fixed while varying the probability of the conditioning event.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes how the conditioning denominator affects the conditional probability, ending with a condition that guarantees the requested event.
findings.checked: All conditioning probabilities are positive and at least 0.12, so each case is feasible. Dividing 0.12 by 0.60, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.12 gives 0.2, 0.4, 0.8 and 1. The unpatterned answer is 0.18/0.45=0.4. The required formula is already taught.
findings.assumptions: Optional additional parts use the existing question instruction.

repair.proposal: After p36-q11-c add: “Predict how the answer will change before calculating.” (d) Find P(A|B) if P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.60. Answer: 0.2. (e) Find P(A|B) if P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.30. Answer: 0.4. (f) Find P(A|B) if P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.15. Answer: 0.8. (g) Find P(A|B) if P(A∩B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.12. Answer: 1. Follow with (h) Find P(E|F) if P(E∩F)=0.18 and P(F)=0.45. Answer: 0.4. In d–g the intersection stays fixed and only the conditioning probability varies.

findings.doneWhen: The four comparison cases and unpatterned follow-up are appended with only the single prediction instruction.

findings.finding: Extend the dice question to compare the evidence supplied by observing a 5 and observing a non-5.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up uses the same reverse-conditional method to show that an observation can reduce the probability of having selected the special die.
findings.checked: P(non-5)=1−5/18=13/18 and P(special and non-5)=(1/3)(1/2)=1/6, giving P(special|non-5)=3/13<1/3. A non-5 has probability 1/2 on the special die and 5/6 on an ordinary die. These calculations use the tree and conditional-probability methods taught by p30.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up to the existing dice question.

repair.proposal: After p41-q25-b add: (c) Given that the die does not show a 5, what is the probability that it is the special die? Answer: 3/13. (d) Is this probability greater or less than the probability of selecting the special die before it is tossed? Explain why. Answer: Less than 1/3, because a non-5 is less likely on the special die than on an ordinary die.

findings.doneWhen: The two optional follow-up parts and their expected answers are supplied.

protectedGroups.observation: Compare how subset, disjoint and overlapping relationships determine intersection, union and complements.
protectedGroups.varies: The relationship between the events; the marginal probabilities also change in part b.
protectedGroups.invariant: The same two-event probability framework and repeated complement and union requests.

protectedGroups.observation: Distinguish A only from B only when the intersection must first be recovered.
protectedGroups.varies: The requested exclusive region and the numerical probabilities.
protectedGroups.invariant: Union and both marginal probabilities are supplied as decimals.

protectedGroups.observation: B only equals all of B precisely when there is no overlap.
protectedGroups.varies: A specified union versus a disjointness condition.
protectedGroups.invariant: The marginal probabilities and the requested event A′ ∩ B.

protectedGroups.observation: The complement always includes everything in the universal set outside A, regardless of B's relationship to A.
protectedGroups.varies: One set, overlapping sets, disjoint sets and nested sets.

protectedGroups.observation: Union combines memberships while intersection retains common membership, including when a component is complemented.
protectedGroups.varies: Union versus intersection, then which component is complemented and the amount of prompting.
protectedGroups.invariant: The underlying overlapping two-set membership regions.

protectedGroups.observation: Complementing the union gives the same region as intersecting the two complements.
protectedGroups.varies: The sequence of operations used to construct the region.
protectedGroups.invariant: The underlying sets and final neither region.

protectedGroups.observation: Combining an intersection with an entire third set differs from restricting a union to A.
protectedGroups.varies: The grouping and placement of union and intersection.

protectedGroups.observation: A union keeps each distinct element once even when the two sets become identical.
protectedGroups.varies: D changes from {3,4,5} to {1,2,3}, increasing overlap to equality.
protectedGroups.invariant: C={1,2,3}, the size of D, and the union instruction.

protectedGroups.observation: Complementing an intersection differs from complementing a union.
protectedGroups.invariant: The universe, the two sets, and the outer complement.

protectedGroups.observation: Each direction of a subset claim must be checked separately.
protectedGroups.varies: The direction of the containment statement.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two sets and the requirement that every element of the first belongs to the second.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing the condition changes the denominator and generally changes the answer.
protectedGroups.varies: Which event is given and which is requested.
protectedGroups.invariant: Population, marginal probabilities and intersection probability.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one marginal probability can change whether the product equals the intersection.
The same marginal probabilities do not guarantee independence when the intersection changes.
Joint probability and conditional probability are different quantities even for the same independent events.
Two equivalent independence tests determine the same unknown frequency.
